title: Tech for Tech's Sake Isn't Good in Our Classrooms
author: Stuart Jr., Dave
summary: Close call, bucketed Ed-Tech rather than Practice & Culture: although it opens with one student's off-task behaviour, the argument is an examination of 1:1 Chromebook adoption itself, asking whether school devices strengthen or erode students' ability to resist distraction. Stuart introduces 'Rachel,' who drifts to new tabs whenever she is on a device, and then resists the easy conclusion that students need device time to be future-ready by pointing to his own literate, knowledge-rich education with minimal technology. He draws on the Hofmann, Vohs and Baumeister desire study, as summarised by Baumeister, to argue that constant access to distraction forces students to spend scarce willpower or lose the depth needed for a process-written essay. He explicitly offers no answers, only a plea that school leaders weigh this research before treating tech for its own sake as progress, likening the pressure to adopt it to an undertow.
points: Stuart challenges the assumption that more devices means better preparation for the future by arguing his own career rests on reading, writing, speaking and knowledge-building, not on hours logged on school computers.
He uses the Hofmann, Vohs and Baumeister beeper study, in which people spent at least a fifth of waking hours resisting desires, to explain why a Chromebook is a willpower drain for students.
The concrete case of a student who skipped turning in an essay to 'finish' it at lunch, while revision history showed it was barely touched, makes the abstract distraction risk visible.
He frames the issue as a question for 1:1 policy makers, whether easy access to school-appropriate distractions strengthens or harms students' capacity for deep work.
The conclusion is deliberately modest, treating 'tech for the sake of tech' like 'new for the sake of new' and urging colleagues to see adoption pressure as an undertow to be wary of.
quotes: One of my students this fall — we'll call her Rachel — has a problem with technology. Whenever she's on a Chromebook, it's as if her fingers take on a mind of their own. She's almost never on task when I come around to see the thesis statement she's supposed to be typing into PollEverywhere, or the Quizlet test she's supposed to be taking, or the Google Classroom task I've assigned.

I'm not a teacher-writer today because of the amount of time I spent on devices in high school. I'm able to do what I do because of how much time my teachers invested in having me read, write, speak, listen, build knowledge, and argue. (My teachers tended toward this approach.) Basically, I graduated literate and knowledgeable with belief that education mattered even if I didn't always love it.

I worry that Rachel's education has been so focused on “engagement” and “differentiation” and “self-actualization” that she's missed a critical mass of opportunities to build lots of knowledge, read and discuss and write about all kinds of things, and along the way develop the capacity to fight off distraction for the sake of deep learning and work.
The researchers concluded that people spend at least a fifth of their waking hours resisting desires — between three and four hours per day.
Such easy access to distraction forces our kids to either use intense willpower or to repeatedly find themselves unable to sustain the depth of thought required for a process-written essay.

I'm not putting forth any answers here. My hope, rather, is to make sure we're thinking about this. Tech for the sake of tech is right up there with new for the sake of new. I understand the pressure toward it, but I'd like it if more of us view that pressure as a kind of undertow, as a thing to be wary of.
